passages.t: A room for Tobiah, and the Levites gone home
passages.happening:
‘At that time the Book of Moses was read aloud in the hearing of the people’ (verse 1), and they find the passage that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, because those peoples did not meet Israel with food and water and hired Balaam to curse them, though God turned the curse around (verses 1-2). ‘As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent’ (verse 3).

Then Nehemiah tells what he found when he came back. Eliashib the priest, ‘a relative of Tobiah’ (verse 4), had given Tobiah a large room in the courts of the house of God, a room that had held the offerings, the frankincense and the tithes for the Levites and singers. Nehemiah had been away: ‘I had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon in the thirty-second year of his reign’ (verse 6). When he returns, ‘I was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room’ (verse 8). He has the rooms purified and the temple's things put back.

He also learns that the Levites and singers have not been given their portions, and that they have gone back to their own fields (verse 10). He rebukes the officials: “Why has the house of God been neglected?” (verse 11). He brings the Levites back to their posts, all Judah brings in its tithes, and he appoints trustworthy treasurers. ‘Remember me for this, O my God, and do not blot out my deeds of loving devotion for the house of my God and for its services’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The book could have ended with the joy of chapter 12. Instead it closes with an honest look at how quickly a community can drift. Nearly every problem Nehemiah meets here is a promise from chapter 10: not to neglect the house of God, not to buy on the Sabbath, not to marry into the peoples around them.

The thirty-second year of Artaxerxes is about 433 BC, after twelve years as governor. Nehemiah returned some time later; the book does not say how long he was away. The Persian king is called king of Babylon because Babylon was one of his capitals, and the title came to the Persian kings after Cyrus took the city.

The temple storerooms were chambers around the courts for the offerings and supplies. Giving one to Tobiah, an Ammonite and an enemy of the rebuilding, turned holy space into a private office for an opponent. And without the tithes, the Levites and singers had no income, since the law gave them no farmland of their own, so they went back to whatever fields they had and the temple's service lapsed.

Eliashib here is probably the high priest of 3:1, though some think he was a different priest in charge of the storerooms.
passages.later: The law read in verses 1 and 2 is Deuteronomy's: ‘For they did not meet you with food and water on your way out of Egypt, and they hired Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you’ (Deuteronomy 23:4). Malachi, speaking to the same kind of neglect, calls the people to ‘Bring the full tithe into the storehouse’ (Malachi 3:10).
passages.hard:
The people excluded everyone of foreign descent when they heard the law about Ammon and Moab. How does that fit with Ruth the Moabite, the great-grandmother of David?

The question is real. Ruth married Boaz and became part of David's line. The difference most often named lies in faith. Ruth took Israel's God as her own, while the concern in Deuteronomy 7 and in Nehemiah is marriage to people who went on worshiping other gods, which had drawn Solomon into sin. On this reading, the issue was faithfulness to God rather than descent.

Still, the chapter raises hard questions about how the exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites was applied, and interpreters differ on how strictly it was meant to work. Later Scripture promises that foreigners who hold fast to God's covenant will be welcomed in his house (Isaiah 56:3-7). The Bible holds both: Nehemiah read the law and acted on it, and the book of Ruth kept the memory of a Moabite who belonged.
passages.asks: A priest made room in God's house for the man who had fought against it. Ask what you have made room for in your life that does not belong there. And ask who has been left without support because others neglected what they had promised.

passages.t: The gates shut for the Sabbath
passages.happening:
‘In those days I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath and bringing in grain and loading it on donkeys, along with wine, grapes, and figs’ (verse 15). Men of Tyre living in the city sell fish and goods to the people of Judah on the Sabbath (verse 16).

Nehemiah rebukes the nobles of Judah for profaning the Sabbath, and he reminds them that their fathers did the same and brought disaster on the city (verses 17-18).

‘When the evening shadows began to fall on the gates of Jerusalem, just before the Sabbath, I ordered that the gates be shut and not opened until after the Sabbath’ (verse 19). He posts his own servants at the gates. When traders camp outside the wall once or twice, he warns them off, and they do not come back on the Sabbath (verses 20-21). He tells the Levites to purify themselves and guard the gates, and he prays, ‘Remember me for this as well, O my God, and show me mercy according to Your abundant loving devotion’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Sabbath rest was one of the clearest marks of Israel's identity. The word comes ten times in this chapter. In a city becoming a busy market, the pressure to trade was strong, especially with foreign merchants like the men of Tyre, a Phoenician trading city, who did not keep the Sabbath themselves.

Nehemiah's remedy is practical: shut the gates at dusk, when the Sabbath began, and keep them shut until it ended. And he treats the matter as serious. To profane, chalal, is to treat something holy as ordinary. He sees Sabbath-breaking as a repeat of the sins that led to the exile.

His prayer is not a boast. He asks God to show him mercy, according to God's loving devotion.
passages.later: Jeremiah had warned Jerusalem in the same terms before the exile: ‘You must not carry a load out of your houses or do any work on the Sabbath day’ (Jeremiah 17:22). The people's own pledge had said, ‘we will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day’ (Nehemiah 10:31).
passages.asks: The people promised to keep the Sabbath, and within a few years the market had taken it over. Ask what has crowded out rest and worship in your own week. And ask what gate you might need to shut, kindly and firmly, to keep a day holy.

passages.t: The marriages, and a last prayer
passages.happening:
‘In those days I also saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab’ (verse 23). ‘Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah’ (verse 24).

Nehemiah tells what he did, without softening it: ‘I rebuked them and called down curses on them. I beat some of these men and pulled out their hair’ (verse 25). He makes them swear not to give their daughters to the peoples around them or take their daughters for their sons. He reminds them of Solomon, who ‘was loved by his God, who made him king over all Israel’ (verse 26), and who was still drawn into sin by foreign women. Even a grandson of the high priest had become Sanballat's son-in-law, and Nehemiah drives him away (verse 28).

He purifies the priests and Levites from everything foreign and assigns their duties, and he arranges for the wood offering and the firstfruits. The book ends with his prayer: ‘Remember me, O my God, with favor’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The complaint about the children's language shows why the marriages were more than a private matter in this small community. Losing the language of Judah meant losing access to the Scriptures and to the community's worship and identity.

Nehemiah's example is Solomon, whose foreign wives turned his heart to other gods. The concern, as in Ezra, is faithfulness to God. The marriage of the high priest's grandson to the daughter of Sanballat, governor of the rival province, tied the priestly family to the political leader of Judah's chief opponent.

Nehemiah contends with the men as in a legal dispute; the word is the one used for bringing a charge. He tells of his own harsh acts plainly, and the text reports them without comment.

The book ends without a celebration. A tired leader is still working, and he asks God to remember him with favor. The walls stand, but the hearts of the people inside them have not been made new.
passages.later: Nehemiah's question echoes Ezra's crisis a generation before: ‘Must we now hear that you too are doing all this terrible evil and acting unfaithfully against our God by marrying foreign women?’ (verse 27), as in Ezra 9 and 10. Malachi charges the priests of the same era: ‘You have violated the covenant of Levi’ (Malachi 2:8).
passages.hard:
Was Nehemiah right to beat people and pull out their hair?

Verse 25 tells how Nehemiah cursed, beat and pulled the hair of men who had married foreign women. The text reports this without comment, and readers should not assume that everything a person in the Bible does is approved. A story describes what happened; it does not by that fact recommend it.

Readers weigh it in two ways. Some see the harsh but lawful discipline of a governor facing a threat to the community's survival, in a culture where public shaming was a normal punishment. Others see a zealous leader whose methods went beyond what was right, and they notice that the book ends with Nehemiah asking for mercy rather than claiming to be in the right. These notes take no side between them.

On one thing there is no doubt. Nothing in this chapter gives anyone today a warrant to strike, shame or harm anyone, at home, in a church or anywhere else, for any cause.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The book ends with a prayer to be remembered, not with a victory. Ask what you will want God to remember when your own work is done. And ask whether your zeal for what is right has ever made you harsh with people.
